title: From white phosphorus to the safety match: phossy jaw, the 1888 London match workers' strike, and the 1906 Bern convention

sources.title: Friction Matches Were a Boon to Those Lighting Fires–Not So Much to Matchmakers

facts.text: English pharmacist John Walker made the first friction match by accident in 1826, when a stick coated with a chemical paste caught fire as he scraped it.
Walker began selling his friction lights in April 1827 and never patented them.
Later experiments produced matches containing white phosphorus, and match-making spread to hundreds of factories in England.
Strike-anywhere matches carry phosphorus in the match head itself.
Most match factory workers were women and children, and they often worked 12 to 16 hours a day.
Breathing white phosphorus fumes could cause phossy jaw: the jawbone died, the teeth decayed, and some workers lost part of the jaw.
About 11 percent of workers exposed to phosphorus fumes developed phossy jaw, on average about five years after they were first exposed.
The first case of phossy jaw was described in 1845; about one in five cases ended in death, often from infection.
At the Bryant & May match factory in Bow, London, workers as young as 14 were employed, and foremen fined workers for things such as dirty feet, an untidy bench, or talking.
In 1888, after a worker was sacked, 1,400 women at Bryant & May walked out on strike, and a few days later the whole factory had stopped.
The strike ended when the workers won their immediate demands: the sacked worker was taken back and the company stopped cutting their pay.
After the strike the workers formed a union, the Union of Women Match Workers, which later became the Matchmakers' Union.
The year after the match strike, London gas workers and dock workers also went on strike; together these strikes became known as New Unionism.
In 1901 Bryant & May announced it would stop using white phosphorus, and a government ban in Britain followed a few years later.
A convention agreed at Bern in 1906 bound the countries that signed it to ban making, importing, and selling matches that contain white (yellow) phosphorus.
In 1919 the first International Labour Conference recommended that all member states join the 1906 white phosphorus convention.
The move away from white phosphorus in matches brought phossy jaw under control; it took about 60 years from the first case to an international convention and laws.
Safety matches were invented in the mid-1800s and soon became the norm.
In a safety match, the phosphorus (red phosphorus) is in the striking strip on the box, not in the match head, so the match cannot light without touching the strip.
